referred to as regions) (Fig. 1), in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. Kwazulu-Natal is characterized by a subtropical climate with warm, wet summers and cool, dry winters (Fairbanks and Benn, 2000). These two regions differ in terms of their elevation (the Midlands occurring at higher elevations compared to Zululand), their topography (the complex topography of the Midlands contrasts to the flat landscapes of Zululand), and soil type (the Midlands being dominated by deep, humic soils, whereas Zululand is dominated by shallow, sandy soils) (Bazelet and Samways, 2012; Eckert et al., 2022b). The high contrast in environmental conditions between these two regions, allow for an assessment of a wide range of conditions. Study sites were selected across several plantation estates within each region (Fig. 1, Table S1), and were situated within three biotope types: indigenous forest, grassland, and eucalypt plantation blocks (Eucalyptus spp.). Only plantation compartments in a mature growth stage were selected, i.e., >6 years into the rotation. The naturally occurring grasslands are maintained through prescribed burning every 2–5 years and grazing by domestic livestock (SANBI, 2014). For each biotope type, 18 sites were selected to maximize on landscape variation, totaling to 108 sites (Fig. 1), with focus being on a high level of spatial replication rather than temporal replication. Sites occurred within the elevation range of 917–1496 m a.s.l. in the Midlands, and 26–131 m a.s.l. in Zululand, with sites within the same biotope being >250 m apart. Sampling was conducted in the summer months of these regions, January–February 2018 for Midlands, and November–December 2018 for Zululand, when arthropods are most active.

Using pitfall trapping, four 300 ml plastic cups (9.5 cm diameter and 8 cm deep) were placed in $\mathrm { ~ a ~ 2 ~ m ~ } ^ { 2 }$ grid at each site. The rim of the trap was level with the soil surface and filled with 50 ml of 60% ethylene glycol (containing a small amount of detergent to break the surface tension). Traps were left in the field for seven days, after which they were collected. Secondly, arthropods were collected directly using an aspirator within a randomly placed 1 m quadrat of each site. This was conducted for 10 min by two people. Arthropods were also extracted using the Tullgren-Berlese extraction technique from 1 L of collected soil from each site (10 × 100 ml subsamples randomly collected). The soil was placed on top of a 0.5 mm aperture size mesh and left for 7 days to allow soil to dry and arthropods to be extracted into the attached 75% ethanol jar below the funnel. Specimens collected from all sampling methods were sorted into morphospecies $( \mathbf { i . e . } ,$ using external morphological characteristics only, without the use of identification keys) (Oliver and Beattie, 1996) (from here on referred to as ‘species’) and counted. Springtail and ant specimens were identified by taxonomic experts (A. Ndaba – for ants, CJS – for springtails). Springtails were identified to family level and ants to genus level. These taxonomic levels were of sufficient resolution for obtaining certain traits from the literature that do not vary substantially within these taxonomic groupings (section 2.3. Functional traits).

We divided the traits for ants and springtails into three categories: 1) morphological traits, 2) feeding strategy, and 3) habitat position (i.e., microhabitat occurrence). For ants, traits used in the analysis (Table S2) were derived from the literature (eye size, habitat position and feeding strategy) (Table S3) or measured in the laboratory (body length, femur length and darkness of the integument). For springtails, body length was measured in the laboratory, and all other traits (eye size, furca development, feeding strategy and habitat position) (Table S4) were determined using previous work on springtails traits (see Salmon et al., 2014; Raymond-Léonard et al., 2019). This was verified by a taxonomic expert (CJS) and a family-level key to the Collembola of South Africa ([https://collembola.co.za/identification-keys/](https://collembola.co.za/identification-keys/)). Generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) were conducted using the lme4 package (Bates et al., 2014). Biotope type was included as a fixed parameter in all models and plantation estate as a random parameter to account for spatial autocorrelation (Fig. 2). Pairwise Wilcoxon tests for non-parametric data using the pairwise.wilcox.test function with Bonferroni correction were conducted where significant effects occurred. Boxplots were constructed using the ggpubr package (Kassambara, 2017).

ME, RG, JSP and MJS conceived the ideas and designed the methodology. Data collection was performed by ME. CJS identified Collembolan specimens. ME, RG, JSP lead the analyses on the data. The first draft of the manuscript was written by ME. All authors discussed the results and contributed to the final manuscript.
